The core insight centers on how reaction potential evolves under reinforcement, where probability of evocation does not linearly map to actual potentiality. Initially, reaction potential increases steadily, but the probability curve exhibits an asymmetric S-shape—steeper early rise followed by gradual saturation. This asymmetry arises because the underlying growth function sEk approaches an asymptote, slowing progress. When reaction potential exceeds or falls short of the threshold, probability becomes a poor proxy for strength or readiness. Thus, two robust indicators emerge: reaction latency and resistance to extinction. These dual metrics capture behaviorally relevant aspects of habit formation that probability alone cannot describe. The failure mode lies in assuming that p directly reflects R(t); instead, R(t) must be inferred through complementary observables. The mathematical structure reveals a dual nature: probabilistic learning curves are not symmetric, and their interpretation depends on contextual thresholds.
